I am a molecular ecologist interested in the origin and maintenance of marine biodiversity and how humans are impacting this biodiversity in real-time. My lab combines fieldwork and molecular approaches to answer questions of ecological significance that are relevant for local community partners, non-profits, and state and federal agencies for the improved management and conservation of fisheries and natural resources. I strive to conduct research that is community-driven, equitable, and reciprocal in nature and to instill these values in my students, to better serve our communities in Waimānalo, Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi, and the Pacific.

 

Academic Journey: My love for all things marine science started as a young kid, rescuing horseshoe crabs from the receding tides with my dad on the Jersey Shore, and my first formal education was during a one-month summer course for high school students, the Oceanography of the Gulf of Maine, through the Sea Education Association (SEA). I completed my BS in Biology with a concentration in Ecology and Evolution at Cornell University, during which I took classes at the Shoals Marine Lab on Appledore Island in the Gulf of Maine, and was an NSF REU student in Akumal, Mexico. After college, I worked at Cornell for the summer and was first introduced to using molecular approaches to answer ecological questions by Steve Bogdanowicz in Dr. Richard Harrisonʻs lab. I then moved across the country before the next cold winter, and lived and worked on Catalina Island off the coast of California for \~2.5 years as a research technician for the USC Wrigley Marine Science Center under Dr. Kathy Ann Miller - trapping and tagging lobsters, conducting underwater fish and invertebrate surveys in kelp forests, setting up a molecular lab there, and helping visiting graduate students with research projects. I also served as USCʻs science representative for Dr. Anthonly Michaels during the planning process for the Marine Life Protection Act (MLPA) in California.

 

I completed my Ph.D. at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa in Zoology, with a Concentration in Ecology, Evolution, Conservation Biology under the supervision of Robert Toonen and Brian Bowen (ToBo Lab). My dissertation focused on lobster population genetics in Hawaiʻi, California and Baja California, Mexico, and across the Indo-Pacific. I was fortunate to be part of both a lobster trapping research trip and multiple diving research trips to the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument for my work. I also conducted intertidal research on ʻopihi and still look forward to opportunities to explore the intertidal and survey ʻopihi populations with local communities throughout Hawaiʻi. After finishing my Ph.D., I was an NSF post-doctoral research fellow in SOEST at UH Mānoa with Dr. Erica Goetze, working on the population genomics of copepods, trying to assess the impacts of climate change on their populations through time.

 

I started as an Assistant Professor at HPU in 2017, where I teach both undergraduate and graduate courses, and mentor students in research at our lab on HPUʻs Waimānalo-Makapuʻu campus in Waimānalo.
